issues.translation_quote: Puss in Boots
issues.justification: The Russian is plural ('Cats in Boots'), a deliberate absurdity that sets up the later budget joke about cutting the cats. Singularizing it to the fixed fairy-tale title weakens the joke and distorts the logic of the exchange.

issues.source_quote: Коты у меня в смете запланированы, а на сапоги денег нет. - ... - Урезать. - Чё? - Котов.
issues.translation_quote: I’ve got the cats in the budget, but there’s no money for boots. ... Cut. ... The cats.
issues.justification: Because the previous line was turned into singular 'Puss in Boots', the ensuing plural cats/boots joke no longer lands cleanly in English. The comic bureaucratic absurdity is significantly impaired.

issues.source_quote: Познакомился весной парень с девушкой одной
issues.translation_quote: A young man met a young girl in springtime
issues.justification: The source means 'a boy met a certain girl one spring', not 'in springtime' as an adverbial rewrite. The existing line sounds generic and lyrical rather than matching the song’s deliberately simple colloquial wording.

issues.source_quote: Больше ничего известный- неизвестный не сказал?
issues.translation_quote: Did that known-unknown say anything else?
issues.justification: The source plays on 'the known unknown' in a specifically comic colloquial way ('that familiar stranger'). 'Known-unknown' is not idiomatic English and fails to carry the joke.

issues.translation_quote: What happened? — The broadcast is on!
issues.justification: The point is that the loudspeaker/radio relay to the whole building has been switched on. 'The broadcast is on' is too vague and does not clearly convey the accidental public transmission central to the scene’s humor.

issues.translation_quote: Tosya, let’s go check the sites.
issues.justification: 'По объектам' is bureaucratic slang for making rounds/inspecting the facilities. 'Check the sites' sounds modern-corporate and awkwardly literal, missing the Soviet workplace flavor.

issues.translation_quote: legs must be insulated
issues.justification: This is a comic bureaucratic euphemism meaning the legs must be covered up. 'Insulated' is too literal and in English suggests thermal insulation rather than prudish censorship, blunting the joke.

issues.source_quote: Добавьте сюда ещё людей, будет большой, массовый квартет.
issues.translation_quote: Add more people here— it’ll be a big, mass quartet.
issues.justification: The humor lies in the oxymoronic Soviet-bureaucratic phrase. 'Mass quartet' is understandable but not funny in English; it reads as clumsy literalism rather than a comic absurdity. A more adaptive rendering was needed.

issues.translation_quote: time to, as they say, go night-night
issues.justification: The childish 'баиньки' is comic in Russian because of the clash with Ogurtsov’s pompous official speech. 'Go night-night' is too babyish and tonally off in English, creating the wrong comic effect.

issues.translation_quote: Spring Torrents
issues.justification: The standard English title of Turgenev’s work is 'Spring Torrents', but 'вешние' has an old-fashioned flavor echoed by the surrounding dialogue. Here the translation loses the period-literary coloration of the allusion; in context this is not just a bibliographic title but part of the character’s sentimental diction.

issues.translation_quote: With my wholesome collective!
issues.justification: 'Здоровый коллектив' in Soviet office-speak means a sound/healthy team in the ideological sense. 'Wholesome collective' is unnatural and misses the specific bureaucratic jargon being satirized.

issues.translation_quote: With Cucumber
issues.justification: This is a punning deformation of the surname Огурцов. Rendering it as the common noun 'Cucumber' loses that it is a joking misnaming of a person, and sounds overly broad rather than character-based wordplay.

issues.translation_quote: Owsya!
issues.justification: This is an exclamation/name with comic sound value; leaving it as a baffling transliteration gives the English viewer nothing. Since the clown rehearsal is all about performance effect, the failure to adapt or explain is a significant loss.

issues.source_quote: Со всей резкостью! / Со всей прямотой мы заявляем!
issues.translation_quote: With all sharpness! / With all straightforwardness we declare!
issues.justification: These are parodic slogans. The literal calques are not idiomatic and do not sound like mock-official oratory in English, so the satire falls flat.

issues.source_quote: В нашей среде, к сожалению ещё имеет место проявление легкомысленного отношения..
issues.translation_quote: In our environment, unfortunately, there still occurs manifestations of a frivolous attitude...
issues.justification: This is seriously ungrammatical English ('there still occurs manifestations'). Since the line mimics pompous official speech, the translation needed controlled bureaucratese, not broken English.

issues.translation_quote: We can start спокойно
issues.justification: An untranslated Russian adverb remains in the English subtitle, which is a clear transfer error.

issues.translation_quote: just one shot
issues.justification: A 'рюмочка' is a small drink/peg, not specifically a 'shot' in modern bar slang. The choice injects a contemporary register and weakens the period feel.

issues.translation_quote: a lecturer from the Society for the Dissemination...
issues.justification: This cuts off the institutional name and leaves it incomplete. The source refers to the Soviet lecture society (for dissemination of political/scientific knowledge); the unfinished phrase is confusing and loses the real-world context.

issues.source_quote: Пять минут, бой часов раздастся вскоре
issues.translation_quote: Five minutes— the clock will soon strike
issues.justification: The song is famous and highly lyrical; several lines are rendered in flat explanatory prose. Here the loss of rhythm and singability significantly damages the artistic effect of an iconic musical number.

issues.source_quote: С новым годом, с новым счастьем
issues.translation_quote: Happy New Year, with new happiness
issues.justification: This is a fixed festive formula. The calque 'with new happiness' is unnatural in English and repeatedly undermines both idiomaticity and the celebratory tone.

issues.translation_quote: the workers of the original-genre department
issues.justification: This refers to variety performers of the 'original genre' (novelty/variety acts), not literal 'workers' in a 'department'. The phrase is a comic institutional label; the translation is misleading and wooden.

issues.translation_quote: People!.. Ah... helloo!
issues.justification: The drunken lecturer is calling out incoherently. 'People!' sounds bizarrely literal in English; a natural equivalent would be 'Folks!' or just a wavering call. The scene’s comic drunkenness is weakened.

issues.translation_quote: look with an armed eye
issues.justification: This is a set phrase meaning 'with the naked eye' versus through an instrument? Actually here he drunkenly mangles scientific language; 'вооружённым глазом' means 'with the aided eye' (through optics). 'Armed eye' is nonsensical in English and fails to reproduce the joke intelligibly.

issues.translation_quote: The Ensemble of Pension and Dance!
issues.justification: The joke is that he accidentally says 'pensions' instead of 'songs'. 'Pension and Dance' is not an intelligible English slip and does not reproduce the malapropism effectively.

issues.translation_quote: Fanfan the Tulip with Onegin
issues.justification: The Russian lists costumed suitors in apposition; 'with Onegin' incorrectly implies accompaniment rather than a list ('Fanfan the Tulip, Onegin, Romeo, a musketeer').

issues.translation_quote: No one is allowed to be bored at our party!
issues.justification: The source is a jaunty carnival rhyme. The translation sounds like a rule or prohibition, losing the festive playful tone.

issues.translation_quote: Undermining authority!
issues.justification: In context this means undermining his authority/status, not abstract authority in general. The line is comic because it is petty and self-important; the mistranslation weakens characterization.

issues.source_quote: И всё же, басня-это хорошо, басня-это сатира. Нам Гоголи-Щедрины нужны!
issues.translation_quote: Still, a fable is good—a fable is satire. We need our Gogols and Shchedrins!
issues.justification: The phrase alludes to the fixed pairing 'Gogol and Shchedrin' as satirists, with comic official bombast. 'Gogols and Shchedrins' pluralized as common nouns sounds odd and misses the rhetorical cliché.

issues.translation_quote: Relying on certain participants of amateur performance
issues.justification: This is very awkward English; 'participants in the amateur troupe' or similar was needed. The current wording sounds machine-translated during a climactic comic scene.

issues.translation_quote: using my direct entry into a box—correct— under the guise of the illusion of being transported through the air in this box
issues.justification: The source text is truncated in the prompt, but the translation here clearly invents connective material ('correct—under the guise...') not supported by the visible source. This is an unjustified addition.

issues.translation_quote: Are those costumes from the theater?
issues.justification: Understandable, but slightly awkward. More natural spoken English would be 'Are these costumes from the theater?'.

issues.translation_quote: It’s untypical!
issues.justification: The literalism preserves meaning but not idiomatic English. 'That’s not typical' or a more characterful recurrent catchphrase would sound better.

issues.translation_quote: employ imaginative play
issues.justification: Stiff and unnatural. The phrase should be something like 'use our imagination'.

issues.translation_quote: Three cubes for that boarding.
issues.justification: Overly literal and obscure. Even if kept technical, the line needs more natural phrasing in English to be comprehensible.

issues.source_quote: Подготовить хороший вечер - это дело не шуточное!
issues.translation_quote: Putting on a good evening is no joking matter!
issues.justification: Serviceable, but 'a good evening' is not idiomatic in English for an event. 'A good party/show' would sound more natural.

issues.translation_quote: Why did you cut off the Shakespeare broadcast?
issues.justification: Comprehensible but awkward; 'Why'd you stop the Shakespeare transmission?' or 'cut off Shakespeare?' would be more natural spoken English.

issues.translation_quote: come here
issues.justification: Natural enough, but the rest of the sentence around it is somewhat clunky and could better reflect Aunt Dusya's conversational tone.

issues.translation_quote: Quite a speech!
issues.justification: The irony is softened. A sharper English equivalent like 'Quite the speech!' would better match Lena's teasing tone.

issues.translation_quote: So-so. The wall spaces are empty.
issues.justification: 'Ничего' here is more like 'Not bad.' 'So-so' is more negative than the source.

issues.translation_quote: Next...
issues.justification: Functional, but a fuller spoken equivalent like 'Let's move on' would fit the dialog better.

issues.translation_quote: A widower.
issues.justification: Accurate, but a little blunt in English. Given the flirtatious, self-pitying tone, it might be integrated more naturally into the sentence.

issues.source_quote: Ничего, только простенки пустые. Зря картину не взяли
issues.translation_quote: So-so. The wall spaces are empty. Should’ve gotten that painting
issues.justification: The connective logic is slightly off; 'Too bad we didn’t get that painting' would track better.

issues.translation_quote: we don’t spend such funds on training so that you can go around tossing economists
issues.justification: Accurate enough but stiff. The phrase sounds translated rather than spoken.

issues.translation_quote: a serious repertoire
issues.justification: The misspelled/pronounced 'сурьёзный' is part of Ogurtsov's comic speech. The translation loses this recurring verbal quirk.

issues.translation_quote: a man of a calm disposition
issues.justification: Naturalized but somewhat flattens the slightly comic, odd phrasing of the Russian.

issues.source_quote: блеснуть, так сказать, по этой линии
issues.translation_quote: Shine, so to speak, along that line!
issues.justification: Literal and awkward. The intended meaning is 'show your talents in that department' or similar.

issues.translation_quote: Well then, shall we hear the clowns?
issues.justification: Understandable, but 'hear' is a bit odd when introducing a visual act; 'let's see the clowns' would be more natural.

issues.translation_quote: Comrades, come in.
issues.justification: Correct, but repeated 'comrades' throughout can sound stiff in English unless strategically varied; here it is slightly heavy.

issues.translation_quote: about five people
issues.justification: The colloquial 'пяток' is roughly right as 'five or so', but some of the flavor is lost; not serious, just flatter.

issues.translation_quote: a city council deputy
issues.justification: Understandable, but 'deputy to the city council' or 'city council deputy' may be acceptable; still, the Soviet institutional feel is only partially conveyed.

issues.translation_quote: Objective circumstances!
issues.justification: Literal and a little odd in English. The joking pseudo-official tone would work better as 'Mitigating circumstances!' or similar.

issues.translation_quote: LOUD, PROLONGED APPLAUSE
issues.justification: The Soviet formulaic stage direction 'friendly prolonged applause' has a specific satirical flavor; the translation loses that political cliché.
